description: Print the kubectl client version and, if a cluster is reachable, the server version.
notes: Keep kubectl within one minor version of the API server; a client more than one minor behind or ahead is unsupported and can silently mangle newer fields. The old --short flag was deprecated in 1.24 and removed in 1.28 - the plain output is already short. Use --client to skip contacting the server entirely.

description: Show the API server endpoint and the addresses of core cluster services.
notes: This is the fastest way to confirm which cluster your current context actually points at before you run something destructive. It only proves the control plane answers - it says nothing about node health.

description: Print the merged kubeconfig that kubectl is actually using, with credentials redacted.
notes: --minify trims the output to just the current context, which is what you usually want. Secrets are shown as REDACTED unless you add --raw. If KUBECONFIG lists several files, this shows the merged result - which is often the explanation for a context you did not expect.

description: Print the merged kubeconfig including client certificates and tokens in full.
notes: This writes real credentials to stdout. Never paste the output into a ticket or a chat. Combined with --minify it is the standard way to extract a single-cluster kubeconfig to hand to CI.

description: List every context in the kubeconfig and mark the current one with an asterisk.
notes: The NAMESPACE column shows each context's default namespace - a blank there means 'default'. -o name prints bare names, which is handy for shell completion and scripts.

description: Print the name of the context kubectl will use for the next command.
notes: Worth putting in your shell prompt. Most production incidents caused by kubectl start with running the right command against the wrong context.

description: Switch the active context so subsequent commands target a different cluster or user.
notes: This mutates the kubeconfig file on disk, so it changes the context for every shell on the machine, not just this one. If you want a change scoped to one terminal, use the global --context flag per command or point KUBECONFIG at a copy.

description: Change the default namespace for the current context so you can stop typing -n everywhere.
notes: The single most useful kubectl config command. Note it edits the kubeconfig on disk and affects all shells using it. Setting --namespace= (empty) puts you back on 'default'.

description: Create or modify a named context that binds a cluster, a user and a default namespace together.
notes: Handy for making a per-team context against the same cluster. The cluster and user must already exist in the kubeconfig - set-context does not create them, and it will happily create a context that points at nothing.

description: Use an alternate kubeconfig file for a single command without touching your default one.
notes: KUBECONFIG accepts a colon-separated list of files and kubectl merges them, with earlier files winning on conflicts. Keeping prod in its own file and only exporting it deliberately is a cheap and effective blast-radius control.

description: Run one command against a specific context without switching your active context.
notes: Safer than use-context for one-off reads against production, because you cannot forget to switch back. --context and --namespace are global flags and work on every subcommand.

description: List every resource type the cluster serves, with its short name, API group and whether it is namespaced.
notes: This is the authoritative list of what exists on THIS cluster, including CRDs installed by operators. The SHORTNAMES column is where you learn that deployments is 'deploy' and that you can type 'po', 'svc', 'ns', 'cm'.

description: List the names of all namespaced resource types that support listing - the building block for 'show me everything in this namespace'.
example: kubectl api-resources --verbs=list --namespaced -o name | xargs -n1 kubectl get --show-kind --ignore-not-found -n payments
notes: The pipeline in the example is the real answer to 'why doesn't kubectl get all show my ConfigMaps' - `get all` covers only a curated handful of types. Filtering by --verbs=list avoids errors from types you cannot enumerate, and --ignore-not-found keeps the output clean.

description: List every API group/version enabled on the cluster.
notes: Use this to check whether an apiVersion in your manifest is actually served before you debug a confusing 'no matches for kind' error. That error means the group/version is missing here - usually a CRD that is not installed or a beta API removed in a newer Kubernetes.

description: Print inline documentation for a resource or a specific field, straight from the schema the server is running.
notes: Better than the website because it reflects your cluster's actual version and includes CRDs. Field paths use dots and skip list indexes: `kubectl explain pod.spec.containers.resources` works.

description: Print the full nested field tree of a resource without the per-field prose.
notes: The fastest way to find the exact spelling of a deeply nested field - pipe it to grep. Output is large, so always target a subtree (pod.spec) rather than the whole resource.

description: Enable tab completion for resource names, namespaces and flags in your shell.
notes: Supported shells are bash, zsh, fish and powershell. Add it to your shell rc file to make it permanent. Completion queries the API server live, so tab-completing a pod name is also a quick check that your context works.

description: Raise kubectl's log verbosity to see the HTTP requests it makes and the raw responses.
notes: --v=6 shows request URLs, --v=8 adds request and response bodies, --v=9 adds full untruncated payloads. This is how you find out what kubectl is actually asking the API server when a command behaves strangely. Response bodies can include Secret contents, so do not paste them around.

description: List the pods in the current namespace with their ready count, status, restarts and age.
notes: READY is ready-containers/total-containers, so 1/2 means one container in the pod is failing its readiness probe. A non-zero RESTARTS column with a recent timestamp in parentheses is the first sign of a crash loop.

description: List pods with extra columns including pod IP, the node they run on, and nominated node.
notes: -o wide is the cheapest way to answer 'which node is this on'. It works on almost every resource type and adds different useful columns for each - on nodes it shows OS image, kernel and container runtime; on services it shows the selector.

description: List pods across every namespace you have permission to read.
notes: -A is the short form. Note that with -A the NAMESPACE column appears first, which breaks scripts that assume the name is column one. It also ignores any -n flag you pass alongside it.

description: List the common workload and service resources in the current namespace.
notes: Badly named: 'all' is a fixed shortlist (pods, services, deployments, replicasets, statefulsets, daemonsets, jobs, cronjobs, replicationcontrollers). It does NOT include ConfigMaps, Secrets, Ingresses, PVCs, ServiceAccounts, NetworkPolicies or any CRD. Never trust it as a namespace inventory before deleting things.

description: List several resource types in one command, grouped in a single output.
notes: Comma-separated with no spaces. This is the practical version of `get all` - you name the types you actually care about, including CRDs. Add -o wide and it applies to every type in the list.

description: Print the full stored object as YAML, including defaults the server filled in and current status.
notes: This is the ground truth for 'what did the cluster actually store', not what your manifest said. It is not directly re-appliable: strip metadata.resourceVersion, uid, creationTimestamp and status first. Since 1.21 managedFields is hidden by default; add --show-managed-fields to see server-side-apply ownership.

description: Show a human-readable summary of an object plus the recent events referencing it.
notes: The Events section at the bottom is the point - it tells you about failed scheduling, image pull errors and probe failures that never appear in `get`. Events expire (one hour by default in many clusters), so an old broken pod may describe with no events at all.

description: List only the resources carrying a matching label.
notes: Comma-separated selectors are ANDed. Labels are the primary way Kubernetes wires things together, so if a Service has no endpoints, running `get pods -l <the service's selector>` is the fastest way to prove nothing matches.

description: Select resources using set-based label expressions: in, notin, existence and non-existence.
notes: Quote the whole selector so the shell does not eat the parentheses or the '!'. Supported forms are `key in (a,b)`, `key notin (a,b)`, `key` (exists) and `!key` (does not exist). `key!=value` also works in the equality syntax.

description: Add a column listing every label on each object.
notes: The quickest way to discover what you can select on. For Deployment-managed pods you will see a pod-template-hash label - that is what the ReplicaSet uses to own its pods, and it is why selecting on it pins you to one rollout revision.

description: Add one column per named label instead of dumping all labels.
notes: Capital -L takes label keys and makes columns; lowercase -l filters. Objects missing the label show an empty cell rather than being hidden, which makes this good for spotting unlabelled stragglers.

description: Filter on object fields rather than labels, evaluated server-side.
notes: Only a small, per-type set of fields is indexed - for pods that is mainly metadata.name, metadata.namespace, spec.nodeName, spec.schedulerName, status.phase and status.podIP. Anything else returns 'field label not supported'. Supports = , == and !=, ANDed by commas.

description: List every pod scheduled onto a specific node.
notes: The command you run before draining a node, to see what you are about to move. It is filtered server-side, so it is much cheaper than listing all pods and grepping. `kubectl describe node <node>` shows the same list plus resource allocation.

description: Show every pod that is not currently in the Running phase - a quick cluster health sweep.
notes: Add status.phase!=Succeeded to hide completed Jobs, which otherwise dominate the output on any cluster running CronJobs. Remember this still will not surface CrashLoopBackOff - check the STATUS column of a plain get for that.

description: Print the current list and then stream every change to it until you interrupt.
notes: -w is the short form. It appends rows rather than redrawing a table, so the columns drift and old rows stay on screen - many people prefer `watch -n1 kubectl get pods` for a stable view. Use --watch-only to skip the initial listing and see only new changes.

description: Rank pods by how many times their first container has restarted, surfacing the flappiest workloads.
notes: Indexed at [0], so it only considers the first container in multi-container pods - good enough as a triage sweep, misleading for sidecar-heavy pods. Pods with no containerStatuses yet (still Pending) sort as if zero.

description: List deployments with desired, up-to-date and available replica counts.
notes: READY is available/desired while UP-TO-DATE counts replicas already running the newest pod template. UP-TO-DATE lagging behind desired during a rollout is normal; it stalling there is not.

description: List ReplicaSets, including the old ones a Deployment keeps around for rollback.
notes: Each Deployment revision is a separate ReplicaSet; ones scaled to 0 are previous revisions retained per spec.revisionHistoryLimit (default 10). Two ReplicaSets with non-zero replicas means a rollout is in flight or wedged.

description: List services with their type, cluster IP, external IP and ports.
notes: An EXTERNAL-IP stuck on <pending> for a LoadBalancer means no cloud controller is provisioning it - normal on bare metal or kind without MetalLB. CLUSTER-IP of 'None' marks a headless service, which returns pod IPs from DNS instead of load balancing.

description: Show the actual backend pod IPs a Service is currently routing to.
notes: This is the definitive answer to 'my Service returns connection refused'. No endpoints means the selector matches nothing, or the matched pods are failing readiness probes - only Ready pods are listed as ready endpoints. The older `kubectl get endpoints` shows the same idea in a more compact but deprecated form.

description: List ingress objects with their class, hosts, address and ports.
notes: An empty ADDRESS usually means no ingress controller has claimed the object - check that spec.ingressClassName matches an installed IngressClass (`kubectl get ingressclass`). The Ingress object itself does nothing without a controller.

description: List persistent volume claims and the volumes they are bound to.
notes: A PVC stuck in Pending is almost always a missing or mismatched StorageClass, or a WaitForFirstConsumer class waiting for a pod to be scheduled. Check the PV's RECLAIM POLICY before deleting a PVC: Delete destroys the underlying disk, Retain keeps it.

description: List HorizontalPodAutoscalers with their current and target metrics and replica counts.
notes: TARGETS showing <unknown> means the HPA cannot read metrics - metrics-server is missing, or the pods have no resource requests set, which is mandatory for CPU-percentage targets. Use describe hpa to see the scaling events and the reason.

description: List PodDisruptionBudgets and how many disruptions they currently allow.
notes: ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS of 0 is exactly why your `kubectl drain` is hanging. A PDB with minAvailable equal to the replica count can block node maintenance forever - check this before blaming the drain.

description: Create or update resources so the cluster matches the manifest - the standard declarative workflow.
notes: Unlike create, apply is idempotent and safe to re-run. It records the manifest in a last-applied-configuration annotation and uses it to work out which fields you removed, so fields you never set are left alone rather than reset - that is how apply coexists with an HPA changing replicas.

description: Apply every manifest in a directory tree in one command.
notes: -R is the short form; without it, subdirectories are ignored. Files are applied in alphabetical order, which is why people prefix manifests with numbers when ordering matters (namespace before the things inside it).

description: Apply a manifest fetched directly over HTTP(S).
notes: Convenient for installing operators, but you are executing whatever is at that URL against your cluster today - always pin a tag or commit rather than a branch, and read the manifest first on anything you care about.

description: Read the manifest from standard input, so you can pipe or heredoc a resource without creating a file.
example:
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: demo
data:
  greeting: hello
EOF
notes: The `-f -` form works on apply, create, delete, replace and diff. It is the standard way to chain generators: `kubectl create ... --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -`.

description: Build a kustomization directory and apply the result to the cluster.
notes: The directory must contain a kustomization.yaml. kubectl ships its own (usually older) copy of kustomize, so a feature that works with the standalone `kustomize` binary may not work here - check `kubectl version` against the kustomize changelog if a build behaves differently.

description: Render a kustomization to YAML on stdout without touching the cluster.
notes: Always render before applying when you are unsure what an overlay does - patches and name prefixes make the output quite different from the base. Pipe into `kubectl diff -f -` to preview against the live cluster.

description: Render what kubectl would send, without contacting the cluster to validate or persist it.
notes: Client dry-run only checks that the YAML parses locally - it will happily accept a nonexistent field or an unknown kind. For real validation you want --dry-run=server. The old --dry-run boolean and -o yaml pairing was replaced by this three-valued flag in 1.18.

description: Send the request to the API server for full validation and admission processing, but do not persist anything.
notes: This is the real preflight check: it runs schema validation, defaulting, and validating admission webhooks, so it catches bad field names, policy rejections and quota problems that client dry-run misses. Mutating webhooks run too, so the returned object shows what would actually be stored.

description: Show what applying a manifest would change, as a diff against the live objects.
notes: The review step before every apply. It exits 1 when there are differences and 0 when there are none, so wrap it carefully under `set -e` in CI. It runs a server-side dry run under the hood, so the diff includes server defaulting and mutating webhooks. Set KUBECTL_EXTERNAL_DIFF to use your own diff tool.

description: Apply using server-side apply, so the API server tracks field ownership instead of relying on a client-side annotation.
notes: Server-side apply records which manager owns which field in metadata.managedFields, giving real conflict detection when two controllers fight over a field. It also avoids the annotation size limit that breaks client-side apply on very large CRDs. Conflicts are errors until you add --force-conflicts.

description: Take ownership of fields another field manager currently owns during a server-side apply.
notes: This deliberately overrides another controller's claim on a field. If that controller is an operator or an HPA, it will likely fight you back on its next reconcile - understand why the conflict exists before forcing it.

description: Create resources from a manifest, failing if they already exist.
notes: Use apply for anything you will update again. create is right when 'already exists' should be an error - and it is the only option for objects with generateName, which apply cannot handle because there is no stable name to match on.

description: Overwrite an existing object wholesale with the contents of the manifest.
notes: Unlike apply, replace is a full overwrite: any field not present in your file is removed, including ones a controller set. The manifest must carry a current metadata.resourceVersion, so the usual pattern is `kubectl get ... -o yaml > f && edit && kubectl replace -f f`.

description: Delete the existing object and recreate it from the manifest.
notes: This is a delete plus a create, not an update - the object gets a new UID, and for a Pod that means downtime and lost state. It is the escape hatch for changing immutable fields (a Job's selector, a Service's clusterIP), not a routine update.

description: Create a Deployment imperatively from an image, without writing YAML.
notes: Good for demos and for scaffolding: add --dry-run=client -o yaml to get a starting manifest you then edit. Supports --replicas and --port; note that --port only sets containerPort, it does not create a Service.

description: Use an imperative create command purely as a YAML generator instead of touching the cluster.
example: kubectl create deployment payments-api --image=nginx:1.27 --dry-run=client -o yaml > deployment.yaml
notes: The single best trick for learning manifest structure and for passing the CKAD quickly - you get correct apiVersion, kind and required fields for free. The generated YAML includes empty creationTimestamp and status stanzas that are harmless but worth deleting before committing.

description: Create a single bare Pod from an image.
notes: Since 1.18 `run` only ever creates a Pod - the --generator flag that once made Deployments and Jobs is gone. A bare pod is not restarted or rescheduled if its node dies, so use `create deployment` for anything meant to stay running. `run` is for throwaway debug pods.

description: Create a Service in front of an existing workload, reusing that workload's labels as the selector.
notes: --port is the port the Service listens on; --target-port is the container port it forwards to. Because expose derives the selector from the workload's labels, it cannot go wrong the way a hand-written selector can. --type accepts ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer and ExternalName.

description: Trigger a CronJob immediately by creating a Job from its template.
notes: The correct way to run a scheduled task on demand - it copies the CronJob's job template exactly, so you test the real thing. The Job it creates is independent of the CronJob's history and concurrency policy, so it can overlap with a scheduled run.

description: Create a CronJob that runs on a recurring schedule.
notes: The schedule is evaluated in the kube-controller-manager's timezone (UTC on most clusters) unless the CronJob sets spec.timeZone, which is only available from 1.27. Quote the schedule so the shell does not expand the asterisks.

description: Open a live object in your editor and apply whatever you save.
notes: Set KUBE_EDITOR (or EDITOR) to choose the editor. Changes take effect the moment you save and exit, with no diff and no review - and they are invisible to whatever Git repo owns this manifest, so the next CI apply silently reverts them. Great for triage, bad as a habit. Add -o json if you prefer editing JSON.

description: Apply a strategic merge patch to a live object, changing only the fields you name.
notes: Strategic merge is the default and is Kubernetes-aware: it merges lists of containers by name rather than replacing the whole list, which is what you want when tweaking one container. It only works on built-in types - CRDs have no strategic merge metadata and fall back to needing --type=merge.

description: Apply an RFC 7386 JSON merge patch, which replaces whole lists rather than merging them.
notes: This is the type that works on custom resources. Beware that any array you include replaces the existing array wholesale - patching one container into spec.containers with --type=merge deletes the sidecars. Setting a value to null removes the key.

description: Apply an RFC 6902 JSON patch, an ordered list of explicit add/replace/remove operations.
notes: The only patch type that can delete a specific array element or address a list by index. Paths are JSON Pointers, so / in a key must be escaped as ~1 and ~ as ~0 - annotation keys like kubernetes.io/name become kubernetes.io~1name. A 'replace' on a path that does not exist fails; use 'add'.

description: Patch the scale subresource directly rather than the main object.
notes: --subresource landed in 1.24 and went GA in 1.29; it also accepts 'status'. Patching the scale subresource is what `kubectl scale` does internally and is the correct way to resize a custom resource that implements scale. Older kubectl versions will reject the flag.

description: Add a label to an existing object.
notes: Fails if the label already exists with a different value - add --overwrite to change it. Relabelling a pod can move it in or out of a Service's selector immediately, which is the basis of the manual 'pull a pod out of rotation to debug it' trick.

description: Remove a label by suffixing the key with a minus sign.
notes: The trailing dash is the removal syntax and works the same way for annotations and for `set env`. Removing a label that a Service selects on immediately drops that pod from the Service's endpoints.

description: Label every object of a type in the namespace, or use -l to label a matching subset.
notes: --all means all objects of that type in the namespace, not all namespaces. Use -l to target a subset; combining --all with -l is not meaningful. This is the standard way to backfill an ownership or cost-allocation label across a namespace.

description: Attach an annotation - arbitrary non-identifying metadata - to an object.
example: kubectl annotate deployment payments-api kubernetes.io/change-cause="rollback to 1.4.2" --overwrite
notes: Annotations cannot be selected on, unlike labels, but they have no value-format restrictions and can hold large blobs. Many controllers are driven entirely by annotations (ingress-nginx behaviour, cert-manager issuers), so annotating is often how you configure a third-party component.

description: Change a container's image, triggering a rolling update.
notes: The container name on the left must match spec.template.spec.containers[].name, not the image name - getting this wrong silently changes nothing and reports success on older versions. Use `*=<image>` to set every container. Setting the same tag with a new digest does NOT trigger a rollout; use `rollout restart` for that.

description: Set an environment variable on a workload's pod template, triggering a rolling update.
notes: Applies to all containers in the template unless you narrow it with -c. Use KEY- to remove a variable and --list to print the current ones without changing anything. Every invocation is a new pod template revision, so bumping three variables in three commands means three rollouts.

description: Inject every key of a ConfigMap or Secret as environment variables via envFrom.
notes: Works with secret/<name> too. --prefix namespaces the injected variable names. Note that changing the ConfigMap afterwards does NOT restart the pods - env vars are read once at container start, so you need `kubectl rollout restart` to pick up new values.

description: Print the environment variables currently defined on a workload without modifying it.
notes: A read-only use of a write command - safe to run anywhere. Add --resolve to display the values behind ConfigMap and Secret references rather than just the reference itself, which is worth knowing before you run it on a shared screen.

description: Set CPU and memory requests and limits on a workload, triggering a rolling update.
notes: Requests drive scheduling and are what an HPA's CPU percentage is measured against; limits drive throttling and OOM-kills. Narrow to one container with -c, otherwise it hits all of them including sidecars. Pass an empty value (--limits=cpu=0) to remove a limit.

description: Change the selector on a Service so it routes to a different set of pods.
notes: The mechanism behind a manual blue/green cutover: flip the Service selector between two label values and traffic moves instantly. Effective immediately with no rollout, and equally instant if you point it at labels nothing has - always confirm with `kubectl get endpointslices` afterwards.

description: Print the manifest that was most recently applied to an object, as recorded in its annotation.
notes: Shows what the last `kubectl apply` sent, which is often very different from the current live object after someone ran edit or patch. Diffing this against `get -o yaml` is a quick way to spot out-of-band changes. Objects created with server-side apply or with create do not have this annotation.

description: Set the replica count of a Deployment, StatefulSet, ReplicaSet or ReplicationController.
notes: Takes effect immediately. If an HPA manages this workload it will simply overwrite your number at its next evaluation, usually within 15-30 seconds - scale the HPA's min/max instead, or the change will not stick.

description: Stop a workload without deleting it, by scaling it down to no replicas.
notes: The polite way to take something offline: the object, its config and its history all survive, so scaling back up restores it exactly. Remember the previous replica count before you do this, because nothing records it for you.

description: Scale only if the workload currently has the replica count you expect.
notes: A cheap optimistic-concurrency guard for scripts: if something else already changed the count, the command fails rather than clobbering it. Well worth using in any automation that scales production.

description: Scale every workload of a type in a namespace at once.
notes: The standard 'shut down the whole environment overnight' command, and equally the standard way to take out a namespace by mistake. There is no confirmation and no record of the previous counts - capture them first with `kubectl get deploy -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,R:.spec.replicas`.

description: Create a HorizontalPodAutoscaler targeting a workload's average CPU utilisation.
notes: The percentage is measured against the pods' CPU *requests*, so a workload with no CPU request can never be autoscaled this way and the HPA will report <unknown>. This generates an autoscaling/v1-shaped HPA; for memory or custom metrics you need to write the v2 manifest yourself.

description: Watch a rollout until it completes, then exit zero - or non-zero if it fails.
notes: The right way to gate a CI pipeline on a deploy actually succeeding. Without --timeout it blocks indefinitely on a stuck rollout, which will hang your pipeline; with it, the command exits non-zero when the deadline passes. Use --watch=false for a single status snapshot.

description: List the revisions of a workload that you can roll back to.
notes: The CHANGE-CAUSE column is populated from the kubernetes.io/change-cause annotation and is empty unless someone set it - the old --record flag that filled it automatically is deprecated and gone. Revisions are stored as ReplicaSets, capped by spec.revisionHistoryLimit (default 10).

description: Show the full pod template stored for one specific revision.
notes: This is how you check what image and env a revision actually contained before rolling back to it - do this rather than assuming revision 4 is the version you remember.

description: Roll a workload back to its previous revision.
notes: The fastest incident response you have. Note it rolls back only the pod template - ConfigMaps, Secrets and database migrations do not come back with it, which is why a rollback of an app that already migrated the schema can make things worse. The undo itself becomes a new revision number.

description: Roll back to a specific numbered revision rather than the immediately previous one.
notes: Confirm the revision's contents with `rollout history --revision=<n>` first. --to-revision=0 is the explicit way to say 'the previous one', which is the default. Revisions older than revisionHistoryLimit have been garbage collected and are simply not available.

description: Perform a rolling restart of every pod in a workload without changing its spec.
notes: Works by stamping a kubectl.kubernetes.io/restartedAt annotation on the pod template, so it honours your rolling update strategy and surge/unavailable settings rather than dropping everything at once. This is how you make pods pick up a changed ConfigMap or Secret, or re-pull a mutable tag like :latest.

description: Freeze a Deployment so spec changes do not trigger new rollouts.
notes: Lets you batch several edits (image, env, resources) into one rollout instead of three, and is also a canary tool - pause mid-rollout to hold a mixed set of old and new pods while you watch metrics. A paused deployment silently ignores your changes until resumed, which confuses whoever finds it next.

description: Unfreeze a paused Deployment and let the accumulated changes roll out.
notes: Everything you changed while paused rolls out as a single revision. If you forgot what was queued, check with `kubectl diff` or compare `rollout history` against the live spec before resuming.

description: Track a StatefulSet rollout, which updates pods in reverse ordinal order.
notes: StatefulSets update from the highest ordinal down and wait for each pod to become Ready before proceeding, so a pod that never becomes Ready blocks the whole rollout permanently. spec.updateStrategy.rollingUpdate.partition can pin the update to only the highest ordinals - a built-in canary for stateful workloads.

description: The first command to run on any misbehaving pod: shows container state, probe config, volumes and recent events.
notes: Read three things in order: State/Last State (with the exit code and reason), the Events list at the bottom, and the Conditions block. Exit code 137 means SIGKILL - usually an OOM kill, confirmed by Reason: OOMKilled. Exit code 1 is the app itself failing, so go to the logs.

description: Read the pod's full status block, including per-container state, restart counts and conditions.
notes: status.containerStatuses[].lastState.terminated holds the exit code and reason of the previous run - the machine-readable version of what describe summarises. status.conditions tells you whether the failure is scheduling (PodScheduled false) or readiness (ContainersReady false).

description: Attach an ephemeral debug container to a running pod, sharing its namespaces, without restarting it.
notes: The correct answer to 'the container has no shell'. --target shares the process namespace with that container so you can see and strace its processes; without --target you only share the network namespace. Ephemeral containers cannot be removed - they stay on the pod until it is deleted - and they cannot declare resource requests or ports.

description: Make a copy of a running pod with a debug container added, leaving the original untouched.
notes: Use this when the pod is serving traffic and you do not want to disturb it - the copy has the same spec but is not behind the Service, since it lacks the ReplicaSet's pod-template-hash label. --share-processes makes all containers' processes visible. The copy is a bare pod you must delete yourself.

description: Copy a pod but replace one container's command, for example to stop a crash-looping entrypoint and get a shell instead.
notes: The way into a container that crashes on startup: same image, same env, same mounts, but it sits at a shell instead of dying. You can then run the real entrypoint by hand and watch it fail properly.

description: Start a privileged debug pod on a node with the host filesystem mounted, for node-level troubleshooting.
notes: The node's root filesystem appears at /host inside the container, and the pod shares the host's network, PID and IPC namespaces - `chroot /host` gives you an effective node shell without SSH. This is a highly privileged operation that most clusters restrict via Pod Security admission, and the debug pod stays until you delete it.

description: Apply a predefined security and capability profile to the debug container.
notes: Profiles are legacy, general, baseline, restricted, netadmin and sysadmin. 'netadmin' adds NET_ADMIN and NET_RAW so tcpdump and iptables work; 'restricted' satisfies the restricted Pod Security Standard, which is what you need on a locked-down cluster. Went GA in 1.28.

description: Launch a throwaway pod, drop into a shell, and have it deleted automatically when you exit.
notes: The workhorse for testing DNS, connectivity and Service reachability from inside the cluster. --rm only cleans up if the command exits normally - if your terminal dies, the pod is orphaned, so check for leftovers. --restart=Never makes it a bare Pod rather than something that respawns.

description: Show live CPU and memory usage per pod.
notes: Requires metrics-server; without it you get 'error: Metrics API not available'. These are current point-in-time readings from the kubelet, not historical data and not the same as what your monitoring stack shows. --sort-by accepts cpu or memory.

description: Show CPU and memory usage per node, with percentages of allocatable capacity.
notes: This is actual usage. It is not the same as what the scheduler sees, which is the sum of pod *requests* - a node can show 20% CPU usage here and still refuse to schedule anything because requests are fully committed. Compare against `kubectl describe node` for the requests view.

description: Block until an object reports a given condition, then exit - the correct way to sequence steps in a script.
notes: Far better than `sleep 30` in CI. Common conditions are Ready on pods, Available on deployments, and Complete on jobs. If the object does not exist yet, wait errors immediately rather than waiting for it to appear - create first, then wait. Exits non-zero on timeout.

description: Wait for every pod matching a label selector to become Ready.
notes: Matches only pods that exist when the command starts, so it will not wait for replicas that have not been created yet - for a deploy, `kubectl rollout status` is the more reliable gate. --all is the equivalent for every object of the type in the namespace.

description: Block until an object has actually disappeared from the API.
notes: Useful after a delete, because `kubectl delete` returns as soon as deletion is *requested*, not when it finishes - terminationGracePeriodSeconds and finalizers can keep an object alive for minutes afterwards.

description: Print every pod's name alongside the restart count of each of its containers.
notes: Unlike --sort-by, this covers every container rather than just the first, so sidecar restarts show up too. A high count that stopped growing is old news; check the container's lastState timestamp to see whether it is still happening.

description: Jump straight to the events on a Pending pod, where the scheduler explains why it will not place it.
example: kubectl describe pod payments-api-7d9f8-x2klm | grep -A 10 Events
notes: FailedScheduling messages name the exact reason per node: 'Insufficient cpu', 'node(s) had untolerated taint', 'didn't match Pod's node affinity', 'had volume node affinity conflict'. Those strings tell you whether to fix requests, tolerations, affinity or storage zone placement.

description: Force a fresh discovery request instead of reading kubectl's local cache of the cluster's API surface.
notes: kubectl caches discovery data under ~/.kube/cache for ten minutes. If you just installed a CRD and kubectl still says 'the server doesn't have a resource type', this is why - either use --cached=false or delete ~/.kube/cache/discovery.

description: Print the stdout and stderr of a pod's container.
notes: Only shows what the container wrote to stdout/stderr - an app logging to a file inside the container is invisible here. Logs are stored on the node and rotated by the kubelet, so they are lost when the pod is deleted or the node is replaced.

description: Stream a container's logs live until you interrupt.
notes: The stream ends when the container restarts, so a crash-looping pod will keep dropping you out. Combine with --tail to avoid replaying hours of history first: `kubectl logs -f --tail=20 <pod>`.

description: Show the logs of the container's previous, terminated instance.
notes: The single most important flag for debugging CrashLoopBackOff: the current container has just started and has nothing useful in it, while the one that died holds the stack trace. -p is the short form. Only the immediately previous instance is kept - two restarts later, it is gone.

description: Select which container's logs to read in a multi-container pod.
notes: Without -c, a multi-container pod errors and helpfully lists the container names. Init container logs are reachable the same way - naming the init container is the only way to see why an Init:Error pod failed.

description: Print logs from every container in the pod, including init containers.
notes: Add --prefix so each line is tagged with the pod and container it came from, otherwise interleaved output is unreadable. Ordering across containers is not guaranteed to be chronological.

description: Show only the last N lines instead of the entire log.
notes: The default is all available lines when you name a pod, but only 10 lines when you use a label selector. On a chatty service, fetching everything is slow and can hit --limit-bytes truncation, so get in the habit of tailing.

description: Show only log entries newer than a relative duration.
notes: Takes Go durations: 10s, 5m, 2h. Use --since-time with an RFC3339 timestamp when you need an absolute window matched to an incident; the two flags are mutually exclusive.

description: Prefix each line with the RFC3339 timestamp the kubelet recorded.
notes: Indispensable when your app logs without timestamps, or when correlating across pods whose clocks or log formats differ. These are the node's timestamps for when the line was written, not the app's own notion of time.

description: Aggregate logs from every pod matching a label selector.
notes: Defaults to only 10 lines per pod and to at most 5 concurrent pods - raise the latter with --max-log-requests. Use --prefix to tell the pods apart. For serious multi-pod tailing, a purpose-built tool like stern handles reconnects and colouring far better.

description: Read logs from a workload without having to look up a pod name first.
notes: Important caveat: this picks ONE pod from the workload, not all of them - so on a 10-replica Deployment you are seeing a tenth of the traffic and may miss the errors entirely. Use -l with the workload's labels when you need every replica. Works with job/, statefulset/, daemonset/ too.

description: Read the logs of a Job's pod, including one that has already completed.
notes: The output survives as long as the Job's pod object does, which is why deleting completed Jobs too eagerly destroys your only record of a migration. Set ttlSecondsAfterFinished generously rather than cleaning up by hand.

description: List events in the current namespace, sorted by time by default.
notes: A dedicated command since 1.26 (GA in 1.27) and much better than `get events` because it sorts sensibly out of the box and understands --for. Remember events are ephemeral: the API server discards them after about an hour, so an event you did not catch is gone.

description: Show only the events attached to one specific object.
notes: Cleaner than describe when you only want the event history, and it works for any object type - a Deployment's events explain rollout decisions, a PVC's explain provisioning failures. Add --watch to follow new events live.

description: Stream cluster events as they happen.
notes: Leave this running in a second terminal while you deploy - scheduling failures, image pull errors and probe failures appear here in real time, usually before anything shows in `get pods`.

description: List events in chronological order using the classic get-based command.
notes: `get events` is unsorted by default, which makes the raw output nearly useless - this incantation is why so many people have it aliased. Note some events populate .eventTime rather than .lastTimestamp and will sort oddly; `kubectl events` handles that for you.

description: Filter events down to warnings, hiding the Normal noise.
notes: Event types are only Normal and Warning. This is a good cluster-wide health sweep: repeated FailedScheduling, BackOff, Unhealthy or FailedMount warnings point straight at the broken thing.

description: Run a command inside a running container with an interactive terminal attached.
notes: The bare -- separates kubectl's flags from the command; omit it and kubectl tries to parse your command's flags as its own. Use /bin/sh rather than /bin/bash for alpine and distroless-adjacent images, and expect nothing at all to work on true distroless images - use `kubectl debug` there instead.

description: Run a one-off non-interactive command in a container and print its output.
notes: Without -it there is no TTY, which is exactly right for scripts and for commands whose output you want to pipe. Note the command runs directly, not through a shell, so `kubectl exec pod -- echo $HOME` expands $HOME in *your* shell - wrap it in `sh -c '...'` when you need shell features.

description: Exec into a specific container in a multi-container pod.
notes: Without -c you land in the first container listed in the spec, which with a service mesh may not be your app. You cannot exec into an init container - by the time the pod is running, it has already exited.

description: Pipe a local file into a command running inside a container.
example: kubectl exec -i postgres-0 -- psql -U app -d payments < schema.sql
notes: -i without -t is the right combination for piping: adding -t allocates a TTY that mangles binary data and inserts carriage returns. This is the standard trick for restoring a database dump into a pod without copying the file in first.

description: Attach your terminal to the main process of a running container rather than starting a new one.
notes: Different from exec: you see the existing process's output and share its stdin, so anything you type goes to PID 1. Detach with Ctrl-P Ctrl-Q; pressing Ctrl-C can kill the container's main process and take the pod down with it.

description: Copy a local file or directory into a running container.
notes: Requires the tar binary inside the container - it fails on distroless and minimal images. Use -c to pick a container. Files copied in are lost on restart, so this is for debugging, never for configuration.

description: Copy a file or directory out of a container onto your machine.
notes: Remote paths are interpreted as relative to the container's working directory unless they start with /; kubectl strips a leading / and warns about it, which surprises people. Add --retries=-1 for large files over a flaky connection.

description: Tunnel a local port to a port on a pod through the API server.
notes: Binds to 127.0.0.1 only by default, so it is safe on a shared machine. The tunnel goes through the API server, so it is slow, single-connection-per-request and drops when the pod restarts - fine for debugging, never for load testing.

description: Forward a local port to a Service, letting Kubernetes pick a backing pod.
notes: It resolves the Service to a single pod and forwards to that - it does NOT load balance across replicas, so this cannot be used to test balancing behaviour. If the Service has no ready endpoints the command fails immediately, which is itself a useful diagnostic.

description: Let the OS choose a free local port and print which one it picked.
notes: Avoids 'address already in use' when you are forwarding several services at once, or in scripts that run in parallel. kubectl prints the chosen port on its first line of output.

description: Bind the forwarded port to an address other than localhost.
notes: 0.0.0.0 exposes an internal cluster service to your entire network with no authentication in front of it. Occasionally necessary (forwarding from inside a container or a VM), but never leave it running - it is an unauthenticated hole into the cluster.

description: Run a local HTTP proxy that authenticates to the API server for you.
notes: Once running, `curl http://localhost:8001/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods` works with no token handling - kubectl injects your credentials. It listens on localhost only and filters non-local requests by default, which is a deliberate safeguard because anyone reaching it has your full cluster permissions.

description: Reach a cluster Service's HTTP endpoint through kubectl proxy without a port-forward.
notes: The service proxy path takes either a port name or a number after the colon. Handy for poking at dashboards and health endpoints of services that have no Ingress. Add `http:` or `https:` before the service name to force the scheme.

description: Create a ConfigMap from key/value pairs given on the command line.
notes: Repeat --from-literal for each key. Values containing spaces or shell metacharacters must be quoted. ConfigMaps are capped at roughly 1MiB because they live in etcd - large files belong in a volume or an object store, not here.

description: Create a ConfigMap whose keys are filenames and whose values are file contents.
notes: Pointing --from-file at a directory adds every file in it as a separate key, non-recursively. The key defaults to the base filename, and filenames that are not valid ConfigMap keys (dots and dashes are fine, slashes are not) will be rejected.

description: Create a ConfigMap by parsing a dotenv-style file into individual keys.
notes: Different from --from-file: each KEY=VALUE line becomes its own ConfigMap key, rather than the whole file becoming one key. Blank lines and # comments are skipped, and there is no quote processing or variable interpolation - a value of "foo" keeps its quotes.

command: kubectl create configmap <name> --from-file=<path> --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
description: Update an existing ConfigMap from files idempotently, since create alone would fail on an existing object.
example: kubectl create configmap nginx-config --from-file=./nginx.conf --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
notes: The standard idiom for 'regenerate this ConfigMap from disk'. Remember that pods do not restart automatically: mounted volumes update within a minute or two, but environment variables never do - follow with `kubectl rollout restart`.

description: Create an opaque Secret from key/value pairs.
notes: The value lands in your shell history in plain text - prefer --from-file, or prefix the command with a space if your shell is configured to skip those. kubectl base64-encodes the value for you; do not pre-encode it or you will double-encode.

description: Create a Secret whose value is the contents of a file, keeping it out of your shell history.
notes: The safer way to create secrets by hand, and the only sane option for binary material like keys and certificates. Files are read byte-for-byte, so a trailing newline your editor added becomes part of the secret - a classic cause of 'invalid token' errors.

description: Create a Secret with one key per line of a dotenv file.
notes: Same parsing rules as the ConfigMap version. Make sure the .env file is gitignored - this pattern makes it very easy to commit real credentials by accident.

description: Create an image pull secret for a private container registry.
notes: Creating it is only half the job - reference it in the pod spec's imagePullSecrets or attach it to the ServiceAccount with `kubectl patch sa default -p '{"imagePullSecrets":[{"name":"ghcr-pull"}]}'`. Pull secrets are namespaced, so each namespace needs its own copy.

description: Create a kubernetes.io/tls Secret from a certificate and private key pair.
notes: This is the shape Ingress controllers expect: keys are exactly tls.crt and tls.key. Use the full chain, not just the leaf certificate, or clients will fail validation. cert-manager creates these automatically, which is nearly always preferable to managing them by hand.

description: Read one value out of a Secret and decode it.
example: kubectl get secret db-credentials -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d
notes: Use base64 --decode on macOS if -d is not recognised. If the key contains a dot you must escape it: {.data.tls\.crt}. The decoded value has no trailing newline, so add `; echo` to keep your prompt tidy.

description: Decode and print every key/value pair in a Secret at once.
example: kubectl get secret db-credentials -o go-template='{{range $k,$v := .data}}{{$k}}={{$v | base64decode}}{{"\n"}}{{end}}'
notes: base64decode is a template function kubectl provides that JSONPath has no equivalent for - this is the main reason to reach for go-template. Obviously this prints live credentials to your terminal; think about who is watching and where the scrollback goes.

description: View a Secret's stored form, with values base64-encoded.
notes: base64 is encoding, not encryption - anyone who can read the Secret can read the credential, and by default etcd stores it unencrypted unless the cluster has encryption-at-rest configured. Read access to Secrets in a namespace is effectively equal to holding every credential in it, so treat RBAC on secrets seriously.

description: Show a Secret's type and the size of each key without revealing the values.
notes: The safe command to run when someone is watching your screen: it lists the key names and byte counts only. Good for confirming a Secret has the keys an app expects before debugging further.

description: Edit a Secret in place; values in the editor are base64-encoded.
notes: You must supply base64 for anything under data. Alternatively add a stringData block with plaintext values - the API server encodes it and merges it over data on save. Pods holding the old value as an env var will not see the change until they restart.

description: Mark a ConfigMap or Secret immutable so it can never be modified again.
notes: Immutability protects against accidental edits and lets the kubelet stop watching the object, which measurably reduces API server load on large clusters. It is one-way: to change the contents you must delete and recreate, so pair it with versioned names.

description: Ask the API server whether you are allowed to perform an action, answering yes or no.
example: kubectl auth can-i create deployments -n payments
notes: Asks the real authorizer, so it accounts for every Role, ClusterRole and any webhook authorizer - much more reliable than reading RBAC YAML yourself. Exits non-zero on 'no', which makes it a usable guard in scripts. Add --quiet to suppress the output and just use the exit code.

description: Print every resource and verb combination you are permitted to use in a namespace.
notes: The single most useful RBAC debugging command - it answers 'what can I actually do here' rather than making you guess at verbs. Add --namespace to scope it; without one it uses your current namespace, not the whole cluster.

description: Check another user's or ServiceAccount's permissions by impersonating them.
example: kubectl auth can-i get secrets --as=system:serviceaccount:payments:payments-api -n payments
notes: ServiceAccounts are named system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>. This is how you verify an application's RBAC without deploying it or extracting its token. You need the 'impersonate' permission yourself, which cluster-admin has; --as-group adds group memberships to the simulated identity.

description: Check whether an identity effectively holds cluster-admin.
notes: Quote the asterisks so your shell does not glob them. A 'yes' for a workload's ServiceAccount is a finding, not a convenience - anything that can create pods cluster-wide can already escalate to the node.

description: Print the username, UID and groups the API server sees for your current credentials.
notes: Added in 1.27 (beta in 1.28). Invaluable with cloud IAM integrations and OIDC, where the mapping from your cloud identity to a Kubernetes username is opaque - this shows exactly which subject your RoleBindings need to name.

description: Apply RBAC objects with correct merge semantics for roles and bindings.
notes: Purpose-built for RBAC: it unions rules and subjects rather than overwriting, and it recreates bindings when an immutable roleRef changes - something a plain apply simply fails on. Add --remove-extra-permissions or --remove-extra-subjects when you want the file to be authoritative rather than additive.

description: Create a ServiceAccount for a workload to authenticate as.
notes: Since 1.24 this no longer auto-creates a long-lived token Secret - pods get short-lived projected tokens instead. If you need a static token for something outside the cluster, use `kubectl create token` or create a Secret of type kubernetes.io/service-account-token explicitly.

description: Mint a short-lived bearer token for a ServiceAccount and print it.
notes: Added in 1.24 as the replacement for the old permanent token Secrets. The duration is capped by the API server's --service-account-max-token-expiration, so you may get back a shorter token than you asked for. The token is printed to stdout - do not log it.

description: Create a namespaced Role granting specific verbs on specific resource types.
notes: Subresources use a slash: pods/log, pods/exec, deployments/scale. Name resources as the plural API name, not the kind. Add --resource-name to restrict a rule to specific named objects, though note that restriction does not apply to list or watch.

description: Create a cluster-scoped Role usable in any namespace or against cluster-scoped resources.
notes: Also supports --non-resource-url for endpoints outside the resource model, e.g. --non-resource-url=/metrics --verb=get, which is what monitoring agents need. A ClusterRole can be bound namespace-wide with a RoleBinding, which is the usual way to reuse the built-in view/edit roles.

description: Grant a Role or ClusterRole to a subject within one namespace.
notes: Use --role for a namespaced Role and --clusterrole to reuse a cluster-wide one, scoped to this namespace. Subject flags are --user, --group and --serviceaccount, and all can be repeated. roleRef is immutable, so retargeting a binding means deleting and recreating it.

description: Grant a ClusterRole to a subject across the entire cluster.
notes: Binding cluster-admin hands over total control of the cluster, including every Secret in every namespace, with no way to scope it down afterwards. Do it deliberately and rarely; a namespace-scoped RoleBinding to the 'admin' ClusterRole is almost always the right alternative.

description: Read out the exact rules a ClusterRole grants, in a readable table.
notes: Worth doing on the built-ins before you use them: 'view' deliberately excludes Secrets, 'edit' can modify workloads but not RBAC, and 'admin' can grant permissions within its namespace - which means admin in a namespace can escalate to anything that namespace's ServiceAccounts can do.

description: List every binding in the cluster with its role and subjects visible.
notes: -o wide is what adds the ROLE, USERS, GROUPS and SERVICEACCOUNTS columns - without it the output is nearly useless. The fastest audit is to grep this for cluster-admin and see who turns up.

description: Apply a Pod Security Standard level to a namespace via the built-in admission controller.
notes: Levels are privileged, baseline and restricted. Use the warn and audit variants of the label first (pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted) to see what would break before enforcing - enforcement rejects non-compliant pods outright, and existing running pods are not re-evaluated, so breakage shows up at the next rollout.

description: Run any kubectl command as another identity, if you hold impersonation rights.
notes: Not just for auth can-i - you can run real commands as another subject, which is the definitive test of whether a workload's permissions are right. Every impersonated request is recorded in the audit log with both identities, so this is traceable rather than sneaky.

description: List nodes with IPs, OS image, kernel version, container runtime and kubelet version.
notes: The first thing to check during an upgrade or a 'works on one node but not another' investigation. Mixed kubelet versions are normal mid-upgrade; mixed kernel or runtime versions are a common explanation for node-specific failures.

description: Filter nodes by label, for example by role, zone or instance type.
notes: Standard labels worth knowing: node-role.kubernetes.io/<role>, topology.kubernetes.io/zone and /region, node.kubernetes.io/instance-type, and kubernetes.io/arch. These are what nodeSelector and topology spread constraints match on.

description: Show a node's labels, taints, conditions, capacity, allocated requests and the pods it hosts.
notes: The densest single view in Kubernetes. Read Conditions for pressure signals, Taints for why nothing schedules, and Allocated resources for how committed the node already is. 'Non-terminated Pods' lists every workload you would disturb by draining it.

description: Mark a node unschedulable so no new pods land on it, leaving existing pods running.
notes: The gentle first step before maintenance. Nothing moves and nothing is disrupted - the node just stops accepting new work, showing as Ready,SchedulingDisabled. Always cordon before you investigate a suspect node so the scheduler stops adding to the problem.

description: Make a node schedulable again after maintenance.
notes: Existing pods do not rebalance onto the node automatically - Kubernetes has no built-in rebalancer, so a freshly uncordoned node stays empty until new pods are created. That is normal, not a bug.

description: Cordon a node and evict all its pods so it can be safely restarted or removed.
notes: --ignore-daemonsets is effectively mandatory, since DaemonSet pods cannot be rescheduled elsewhere and drain refuses to proceed without it. Drain uses the eviction API, so PodDisruptionBudgets are honoured - a PDB allowing zero disruptions will make this hang indefinitely. Pods with local emptyDir data need --delete-emptydir-data and will lose that data.

description: Drain a node and also delete pods that no controller manages.
notes: --force is what deletes bare pods - pods with no ReplicaSet, Job or StatefulSet behind them. Those pods are gone permanently, because nothing exists to recreate them. Check for them first with `kubectl get pods -A --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node> -o wide` and see which have no owner.

description: Add a taint so only pods with a matching toleration will schedule on the node.
notes: Effects are NoSchedule (no new pods), PreferNoSchedule (soft) and NoExecute (evicts existing pods that do not tolerate it, immediately). NoExecute on a busy node is an instant mass eviction, so be sure before using it. Taints repel pods; nodeSelector and affinity attract them - you usually need both.

description: Remove a taint using the trailing-dash syntax.
notes: You can drop the value and remove all taints with a given key and effect: `kubectl taint nodes <node> dedicated:NoSchedule-`. Removing a taint does not pull existing pods back onto the node - only new scheduling decisions are affected.

description: List every node alongside its taint keys, in one table.
notes: Much faster than describing nodes one by one when a pod will not schedule. An empty TAINTS cell shows as <none>. Taints on control-plane nodes (node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule) are normal and intentional.

description: Add a label to a node so workloads can target it with nodeSelector or affinity.
notes: Labels under kubernetes.io/ and k8s.io/ are restricted - the kubelet cannot set most of them, so use your own domain for custom labels. Labelling a node does not move existing pods; only future scheduling decisions consider it.

description: Show each node's Ready condition status in a compact table.
notes: The [?(@.type=="Ready")] filter is a JSONPath predicate - the same syntax works for MemoryPressure, DiskPressure and PIDPressure. A Ready status of Unknown means the kubelet has stopped reporting entirely, which is different from a node that reports itself unhealthy.

description: Remove a node object from the cluster's registry.
notes: This deletes the API object, not the machine - if the kubelet is still running it will simply re-register itself in seconds. Always drain first, then delete, then terminate the instance. Deleting a node object orphans its pods and forces them to be rescheduled.

description: Ask the API server for a per-check readiness breakdown.
notes: Each individual health check is listed with ok or failed, including etcd connectivity and informer sync - far more informative than a plain /healthz that just says 'ok'. /livez?verbose is the liveness equivalent.

description: Show the legacy health summary for scheduler, controller-manager and etcd.
notes: Deprecated since 1.19 and broken or empty on most managed clusters, where the control plane is not reachable at the addresses it assumes. Use `kubectl get --raw '/readyz?verbose'` and your control-plane metrics instead - this command survives mainly in old runbooks.

description: Emit the complete object as YAML, including server-set defaults and live status.
notes: The default output is a summary table; -o yaml is the full truth. To turn it back into an appliable manifest you must remove status, metadata.uid, metadata.resourceVersion, metadata.generation, metadata.creationTimestamp and any cluster-assigned fields like spec.clusterIP.

description: Emit objects as JSON, the format to pipe into jq.
example: kubectl get pods -o json | jq '.items | length'
notes: A list request wraps results in a List object with the objects under .items; a single named request returns the object directly. Handling both shapes is why so many scripts break when they go from one pod to many.

description: Print only type/name identifiers, one per line.
notes: The output is valid input to other kubectl commands, so `kubectl get ... -o name | xargs kubectl delete` works without any parsing. Prefer it over awk-ing column one.

description: Extract a single field from an object using a JSONPath expression.
notes: kubectl's JSONPath is a subset of the full spec: no filters on arbitrary expressions, no functions beyond a few. Output has no trailing newline, so append {"\n"} or `; echo` when you want one. A path that matches nothing prints nothing and still exits zero.

description: Pull one field from every object in a list, space-separated.
notes: [*] iterates a list. Results come out space-separated on one line, so pipe through `tr ' ' '\n'` to get one per line. Use the range form when you need several fields per object.

description: Loop over a list and emit several fields per object as a formatted line.
notes: range/end is the construct that turns JSONPath from a field extractor into a report generator. Literal text goes in double quotes inside the braces, including \t and \n. Wrap the whole expression in single quotes so your shell leaves the double quotes alone.

description: Filter a list with a JSONPath predicate and print a field from the matches.
notes: @ refers to the current element. Supported comparisons are ==, != and the numeric operators; there is no regex and no and/or, so complex filters belong in jq instead. Quote string literals with double quotes inside the single-quoted expression.

description: Read a label or annotation whose key contains dots or slashes, by escaping the dots.
notes: Dots inside a key must be escaped with a backslash, otherwise JSONPath treats them as path separators - and inside a shell single-quoted string that means one backslash, but two if you use double quotes. The alternative bracket form {.metadata.annotations['kubernetes.io/change-cause']} avoids the problem entirely.

description: Define your own table columns from JSONPath expressions.
notes: Cleaner than jsonpath+awk for anything a human will read, and it handles column alignment for you. Paths here are written without surrounding braces. A path that matches nothing renders as <none>. No spaces are allowed around the commas.

description: Build a table of pod resource requests to find workloads with none set.
notes: Pods showing <none> have no requests, which means the scheduler treats them as free and they are first in line for eviction under memory pressure - their QoS class is BestEffort. This one query surfaces most of a cluster's capacity-planning problems.

description: Format output with a Go text/template, for logic JSONPath cannot express.
notes: Use this when you need conditionals, string functions or base64decode - the last of which is the only built-in way to decode a Secret without shelling out. Templates are verbose, so reach for custom-columns first and go-template only when it cannot do the job.

description: Sort table output by any field, ascending.
notes: The expression is a JSONPath without braces, evaluated against each object. Sorting is client-side on the fetched list, and there is no descending flag - pipe to `tac`, keeping in mind that reverses the header row too.

description: Use jq for filtering and reshaping that kubectl's own formatters cannot handle.
example: kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.status.phase!="Running") | "\(.metadata.namespace)/\(.metadata.name) \(.status.phase)"'
notes: jq gives you boolean logic, regex, arithmetic and grouping, none of which JSONPath has. -r strips the JSON quotes from string output. Remember that jq runs on data already transferred, so filtering server-side with a field selector first is cheaper on large clusters.

description: Include the managedFields metadata that records which controller owns which field.
notes: Hidden by default since 1.21 because it is enormous and unreadable. Turn it on when debugging server-side apply conflicts or when you need to know which controller is fighting you over a field - the manager names tell you exactly who set what.

description: Fetch a raw API response and pretty-print it.
notes: Raw output is a single unformatted JSON line, so piping through jq is effectively mandatory. Use this to reach API paths kubectl has no resource type for, or to see exactly what the server returns before kubectl's client-side processing.

description: Delete a named object.
notes: Deleting a pod that belongs to a Deployment or StatefulSet just makes the controller create a replacement - which is exactly the point when you want to restart one misbehaving replica. To actually remove a workload you must delete the controller, not its pods.

description: Delete exactly the resources described in a manifest.
notes: Much safer than deleting by name because the manifest is an explicit, reviewable list of what will go. Add --ignore-not-found so it succeeds when some objects are already gone, which makes teardown scripts idempotent.

description: Delete everything a kustomization renders.
notes: Deletes exactly what `kubectl apply -k` on the same directory would create, which makes environment teardown symmetrical. Render with `kubectl kustomize` first if you want to see the list before it disappears.

description: Delete every object of a type matching a label selector.
notes: Test the selector with `kubectl get` before you run the delete - the two commands take identical selectors, so there is no excuse for guessing. A typo that matches more broadly than intended is the classic way to delete production.

description: Delete every object of one type in a namespace.
notes: --all means every object of that type in the namespace, and there is no confirmation prompt. Always state -n explicitly rather than relying on your current context, because this is precisely the command you do not want to run in the wrong namespace.

description: Delete the common workload and service resources in a namespace.
notes: Misleading in both directions: 'all' is the same limited shortlist as `kubectl get all`, so ConfigMaps, Secrets, PVCs, Ingresses and CRDs survive - while everything running is destroyed instantly. If you truly want the namespace empty, delete the namespace instead.

description: Delete a namespace and everything inside it.
notes: Irreversible and total: every object in the namespace goes, including PVCs, which for a Delete-reclaim StorageClass destroys the underlying disks. Deletion is asynchronous and can take minutes; if it sticks in Terminating, some resource has a finalizer nobody is clearing.

description: Remove a pod object from the API immediately without waiting for the kubelet to confirm.
notes: This deletes the API record, not necessarily the running container - on an unreachable node the process may keep running and keep writing to storage. For StatefulSets that is genuinely dangerous: the controller will start a replacement with the same identity and volume, giving you two writers. Only use it on a node you know is truly dead.

description: Delete with a one-second grace period instead of the pod's configured value.
notes: A middle ground between a graceful delete and --force: the kubelet is still told to stop the container, so you do not risk a zombie process, but you skip a long terminationGracePeriodSeconds. Prefer this to --grace-period=0 --force when you are just impatient.

description: Delete a controller but leave the objects it owns running.
notes: The pods keep running with no supervisor - nothing will restart or reschedule them, and a matching new Deployment may adopt them via labels, which can be either a clever migration trick or a nasty surprise. --cascade=background (the default) deletes children asynchronously; --cascade=foreground waits for them.

description: Delete objects matching a server-side field selector.
notes: The tidy way to clear out completed Job pods that have accumulated. Run the identical `kubectl get` first to see the list. Configure ttlSecondsAfterFinished on your Jobs so you do not have to do this by hand.

command: kubectl get <resource> -o name -l <selector> | xargs kubectl delete
description: Select objects first, review the list, then delete exactly those.
example: kubectl get pods -o name --field-selector status.phase=Failed | xargs -r kubectl delete
notes: The safe pattern: run the `get` alone first and read the output, then add the pipe. -r on xargs stops it running kubectl with no arguments when nothing matched, which would otherwise produce a confusing error.

description: Strip finalizers from an object stuck in Terminating so the API server can remove it.
notes: A last resort. Finalizers exist so a controller can clean up external resources - cloud disks, load balancers, DNS records - and removing them deletes the Kubernetes object while leaving that infrastructure orphaned and still billing you. Find out why the finalizer is not clearing before reaching for this.

command: kubectl get namespace <name> -o json | jq 'del(.spec.finalizers)' | kubectl replace --raw /api/v1/namespaces/<name>/finalize -f -
description: Force-clear a namespace wedged in Terminating by writing directly to its finalize subresource.
example: kubectl get namespace staging -o json | jq 'del(.spec.finalizers)' | kubectl replace --raw /api/v1/namespaces/staging/finalize -f -
notes: Needed because a namespace's finalizer cannot be patched the normal way. Before running it, find the real cause: `kubectl api-resources --verbs=list --namespaced -o name | xargs -n1 kubectl get --show-kind --ignore-not-found -n <name>` lists what is still in there, usually a custom resource whose operator has been uninstalled. Forcing it leaves those objects orphaned in etcd.

description: Remove Jobs that have completed successfully, along with their pods.
notes: Deleting the Job also deletes its pods and therefore its logs, so capture anything you need first. Setting spec.ttlSecondsAfterFinished on the Job is the proper fix - it lets the controller clean up on a schedule instead of you remembering to.

description: Delete a PersistentVolumeClaim.
notes: Whether your data survives depends entirely on the PV's reclaim policy: Delete destroys the underlying disk, Retain keeps the PV around in Released state for manual recovery. Check with `kubectl get pv` before deleting. A PVC still mounted by a running pod will sit in Terminating until that pod goes.

description: Delete a CustomResourceDefinition and, with it, every custom resource of that kind.
notes: Cluster-wide and instant: deleting a CRD removes all its instances in every namespace, with no confirmation and no undo. Inventory them first with `kubectl get <kind> -A`. Uninstalling an operator by deleting its CRDs is how people accidentally destroy every certificate or database in a cluster.

description: Preview which objects a pruning apply would delete before doing it for real.
notes: Always run the dry-run first: prune deletes anything carrying the label that is not in your input, so an empty or wrong directory means it deletes everything the label matches. Prune has been alpha/beta for years, ignores types outside its allowlist unless you pass --prune-allowlist, and is best replaced by a proper GitOps controller.
